rows.replace:
H1: Innrly + Inn-Flow: How the Automation Layer Fits

Inn-Flow is an established hotel accounting and back-office platform, and many multi-property operators already run their books on it. Innrly is not a replacement for Inn-Flow. Innrly is an automation layer that can sit alongside the accounting system a hotel group already uses.

H2: How the two fit together
- Inn-Flow remains the accounting system of record.
- Innrly focuses on the work that happens before entries reach the books: invoice capture, GL-coding suggestions, approval routing, OTA reconciliation flags and portfolio reporting.
- Your accounting team keeps its existing chart of accounts, close process and controls in Inn-Flow.

H2: Integration status
A proposed Innrly integration with Inn-Flow is on our roadmap. It is not live today. Before planning a deployment, contact us to confirm availability, the data that will be supported and the workflow for your properties.

H2: Who this is for
Hotel groups that use Inn-Flow and want to explore extra automation for accounts payable, reconciliation or reporting, without changing their accounting system.

H2: Next step
Talk to our team about your current Inn-Flow setup and which workflows you want to automate. We will tell you plainly what is available now and what is still on the roadmap.

H2: FAQ
Q: Is Innrly a competitor to Inn-Flow?
A: No. We position Innrly as an automation layer that works alongside your accounting system. Inn-Flow stays your system of record.
Q: Is the Inn-Flow integration available now?
A: Not yet. It is on our roadmap. Contact us to confirm current status before planning a rollout.
Q: Do I need to change accounting systems to use Innrly?
A: No. Innrly is designed to work with the accounting system you already use.
Q: Where can I learn more?
A: See the Inn-Flow integration page at /integrations/inn-flow.

rows.find: Labor is the largest controllable cost in every hotel. For most multi-property operators it is 25%–40% of revenue, and it is the line that swings GOPPAR the most quarter to quarter. This guide gives you the right formula, real benchmarks by segment, and the seven levers that lower the number without crushing guest scores.
rows.replace: Labor is one of the largest controllable costs in a hotel, and it can swing GOPPAR from quarter to quarter. This guide covers the formula, how to choose your benchmark, and practical levers that can lower the number without hurting guest scores.

rows.find: Labor cost % = Total labor cost / Total revenue
rows.replace: Labor cost % = (Total labor cost / Total revenue) x 100

rows.find: (add right after the formula)
rows.replace: Decide with your accountant which revenue you use (total vs rooms revenue, gross vs net) and whether labor is wages-only or fully loaded. Use the same definition every month and across every property.

rows.find: Most operators report the simpler version (wages + payroll taxes / rooms revenue) — that's fine for property-level operating reviews but understates true cost by 15%–25%.
rows.replace: Many operators report a simpler version (wages + payroll taxes / rooms revenue). That can be fine for property reviews, but it will read lower than a fully loaded figure. Label which version you use.

rows.find: Industry benchmarks (US, 2025–2026)
rows.replace: Setting your benchmark
DELETE completely.

rows.find: (add where the table was)
rows.replace: Benchmarks vary by segment, market, service level and how labor is defined. Use your own history, your management company's targets or a paid benchmark report, and compare like for like.

rows.find: Benefits inflation. Health premiums rose 8%–12% in 2024–2025 and most operators didn't reprice schedules.
rows.replace: Benefits inflation. When health premiums rise, labor cost % rises even if schedules stay the same. Review schedules when benefits renew.

rows.find: Re-publish schedule 72 hours out using actual booked-on-the-books occupancy. Typical savings: 2–4% of labor cost.
rows.replace: Re-publish the schedule close to the date using on-the-books occupancy.

rows.find: Most scheduling systems can hard-cap OT before the schedule publishes. Typical savings: 1–3%.
rows.replace: Many scheduling systems can flag or cap overtime before the schedule is published.

rows.find: Bridges shoulder periods without adding heads. Typical savings: 1–2%.
rows.replace: Cross-training can bridge shoulder periods without adding headcount.

rows.find: Set MPOR targets per property and flag outliers weekly. See MPOR Explained. Typical savings on housekeeping line: 8–15%.
rows.replace: Set MPOR targets per property and flag outliers weekly. See MPOR Explained.

rows.find: Geofenced clock-in eliminates buddy-punching and early-clock-in drift. Typical savings: 0.5–1.5%.
rows.replace: Location checks and Face-ID punches can help reduce early clock-ins and buddy punching. A location check alone does not confirm who is punching.

rows.find: Re-shop carriers annually. Most hotels overpay 8%–15% by auto-renewing.
rows.replace: Re-shop benefit and workers' comp carriers regularly instead of auto-renewing.

rows.find: What is a good hotel labor cost percentage? Depends on segment: 22%–28% economy, 28%–34% upper midscale, 32%–38% upscale, 40%–48% luxury.
rows.replace: What is a good hotel labor cost percentage? It depends on segment, market, service level and how you define labor and revenue. Compare against your own history and like-for-like properties.

rows.find: Should I include benefits and payroll taxes? Yes for true cost. Wages-only understates by 15%–25%.
rows.replace: Should I include benefits and payroll taxes? For true cost, yes. Wages-only figures read lower. Label which version you report.

rows.find: Most hotel operators track RevPAR, ADR, occupancy, GOPPAR, and labor cost percentage. Very few track MPOR — Minutes Per Occupied Room — and as a result, most multi-property portfolios overpay for housekeeping by 8%–15%.
rows.replace: Most hotel operators track RevPAR, ADR, occupancy, GOPPAR and labor cost percentage. Fewer track MPOR (Minutes Per Occupied Room), which can show where housekeeping time is going across a portfolio.

rows.find: This guide explains what MPOR is, the formula, the benchmarks, and how to track it across a portfolio.
rows.replace: This guide explains what MPOR is, the formula, how to set your own targets and how to track it across a portfolio.

rows.find: It is the cleanest productivity measure for the largest variable labor line in your hotel. Lower MPOR (within quality standards) = better labor productivity. Higher MPOR = either better service or operational waste — usually waste.
rows.replace: It is a useful productivity measure for one of the largest variable labor lines in a hotel. A higher MPOR can mean a higher service level or wasted time, so review it alongside quality scores.

rows.find: MPOR = Total housekeeping minutes worked / Number of occupied rooms
rows.replace: MPOR = Total housekeeping minutes worked / Number of occupied room-nights

rows.find: (add right after the formula)
rows.replace: Choose your denominator and keep it consistent. Occupied room-nights and rooms actually cleaned are different numbers when stayovers are not serviced every day. Some operators track both.

rows.find: Example: - 8 housekeepers × 8 hours × 60 minutes = 3,840 minutes worked - 120 rooms occupied - MPOR = 3,840 / 120 = 32 minutes per occupied room
rows.replace: Hypothetical example: - 8 housekeepers x 8 hours x 60 minutes = 3,840 minutes worked - 120 occupied room-nights - MPOR = 3,840 / 120 = 32 minutes per occupied room-night

rows.find: Industry benchmarks (US, 2025–2026)
rows.replace: Setting MPOR targets

rows.find: The whole benchmark table (Segment / Brand examples / MPOR benchmark: Economy 18-22, Midscale 22-28, Upper midscale 26-32, Upscale 30-38, Upper upscale 36-45, Luxury 50-70)
rows.replace: DELETE completely.

rows.find: If your portfolio MPOR is more than 15% above the segment benchmark, you have a productivity problem.
rows.replace: Set targets from your own history, brand standards and room mix, then investigate properties that move well above their own target.

rows.find: Stayovers (5–10 min) are faster than checkouts (25–40 min). High-checkout days = higher MPOR.
rows.replace: Stayovers usually take less time than checkouts, so high-checkout days raise MPOR.

rows.find: Suites take 1.5–2x the time of standard rooms.
rows.replace: Suites and larger rooms take longer than standard rooms.

rows.find: Daily service vs every-other-day vs on-request changes MPOR by 20%+.
rows.replace: Service frequency (daily, every other day or on request) changes MPOR noticeably.

rows.find: Housekeepers idle between assignments is the silent killer. Bad scheduling adds 4–8 minutes per occupied room.
rows.replace: Idle time between assignments is a hidden driver. Poor scheduling adds minutes to every room.

rows.find: Flag properties >15% over benchmark
rows.replace: Flag properties that are well above their own target

rows.find: Doing this manually across 10 properties = 8–12 hours / month. Doing it in software = 0 hours.
rows.replace: Doing this manually across many properties takes hours each month. Software can do the calculation automatically.

rows.find: What is MPOR? Minutes Per Occupied Room — the average housekeeping minutes spent cleaning each occupied room per day.
rows.replace: What is MPOR? Minutes Per Occupied Room: housekeeping minutes worked divided by occupied room-nights (or rooms cleaned, if that is the denominator you choose).

rows.find: How is MPOR calculated? Total housekeeping minutes worked divided by occupied rooms.
rows.replace: How is MPOR calculated? Total housekeeping minutes worked divided by occupied room-nights. Use the same denominator every time.

rows.find: What is a good MPOR? Depends on segment: 18–22 min for economy, 22–28 for midscale, 26–32 for upper midscale, 30–38 for upscale, 50–70 for luxury.
rows.replace: What is a good MPOR? It depends on segment, room mix, service standards and stayover policy. Set targets from your own history and brand standards.
